question: 让人不舒服的好东西，卖得出去吗？
question_en: Can something good that makes people uncomfortable survive a market?
sub: 如实的体检、不讨好的新闻、会挂科的课、直言的朋友，价值恰在那点不适，供给者却靠你愿意再来。
sub_en: An honest check-up, unflattering news, a course you can fail, a blunt friend: their value lies in the sting, yet the supplier depends on you coming back.

casting.reason: 她是成瘾科医生，亲见过患者满意度评分如何把医生推向多开止痛药。她从大脑的快感—痛苦跷跷板讲起：先甜后苦的东西，天然比先苦后甜的好卖。
casting.reason_en: An addiction physician, she has watched patient-satisfaction scores push doctors toward more painkillers. She starts from the brain's pleasure-pain seesaw: what is sweet first and bitter later will always sell better than the reverse.

casting.reason: 他站在市场一边，却给出一个反直觉的观察：靠学费吃饭的教师比领固定薪俸的更尽心。他认为磨平不适的往往不是市场，而是评价与结果之间的时间错位。
casting.reason_en: He stands on the market's side but brings a counterintuitive observation: teachers who live on fees work harder than those on fixed stipends. What sands discomfort away, he argues, is often not the market but the gap in time between judgement and result.

casting.reason: 他在《说难》里把进言之难讲到极处：话对不对是一回事，听的人受不受得了是另一回事。他不信人心会自己去爱逆耳之言，主张用法度把实话钉进制度里。
casting.reason_en: In 'The Difficulties of Persuasion' he took the danger of advice as far as it goes: whether a thing is true is one question, whether the listener can bear it is another. He doesn't trust anyone to love unwelcome words of their own accord and wants law to nail the truth into institutions.

casting.reason: 他把矛头从卖方转向买方：报纸讨好的『公众』是个没人负责的幽灵，真理只对单个的人说话。他认为不适卖不动，根子在人宁愿被群众安慰。
casting.reason_en: He turns the question from the seller to the buyer: the 'public' that newspapers flatter is a phantom no one answers for, and truth speaks only to the single individual. Discomfort doesn't sell, he says, because people would rather be comforted by the crowd.

casting.reason: 他替市场辩护：健身房、训练营、打卡应用都在卖痛苦，而且卖得不错。他认为关键在付款时刻——让做计划的那个你先付钱，不适就活得下去。
casting.reason_en: He defends the market: gyms, boot camps and habit apps all sell pain, and sell it well. The key, he argues, is when you pay: let the planning self pay up front and discomfort can survive.

casting.reason: 他按『真实、有益、中不中听』给言语分类，只说真实有益的话，且等合适的时机。僧团靠托钵供养而不卖法，他把这当作让说话的人不必讨好听众的一种安排。
casting.reason_en: He sorts speech by whether it is true, beneficial and welcome, says only what is true and beneficial, and waits for the right moment. His order lives on alms rather than selling teaching, an arrangement that frees the speaker from courting the listener.

casting.reason: 他从公共领域的变迁看新闻：读者从讨论者变成消费者，批判就变成了展示。他的解法是制度上的一道墙，让钱和内容分开。
casting.reason_en: He reads the news through the transformation of the public sphere: once readers become consumers rather than participants, criticism turns into display. His remedy is an institutional wall that keeps money and content apart.

casting.reason: 她为苏格拉底式教育辩护，也看见学生被当作『客户』后评教如何压低难度。她补上被忽略的一半：直言要有用，必须先让人感到被尊重。
casting.reason_en: She defends Socratic education and has seen how course evaluations drive difficulty down once students are treated as customers. She adds the half that is usually missed: for candour to work, people must first feel respected.

casting.reason: 他一无所有，所以能叫亚历山大别挡住阳光。他的答案最直接：谁要靠你吃饭，谁就没法对你说真话；想要直言，先把欲望降下来。
casting.reason_en: He owns nothing, which is why he can tell Alexander to stand out of his sun. His answer is the bluntest: whoever eats at your table cannot tell you the truth, so if you want candour, shrink your wants first.

posts.text: 我是看病的。美国曾把患者满意度纳入医院考核，还跟医保支付挂钩，问卷里专门问『疼痛控制得好不好』。于是多开阿片类止痛药成了换好评最省事的办法：病人当场舒服，账单十年后才来——成瘾、过量、死亡。**大脑会把一句难听的实话当成一次小小的痛，本能地躲开；而市场最擅长的，就是替你躲开。**快感和痛苦压在同一架跷跷板上，先甜后苦的东西，永远比先苦后甜的好卖。
posts.text_en: I'm a doctor. America once folded patient satisfaction into hospital ratings and tied it to Medicare payments, and the survey asked specifically how well your pain was controlled. Prescribing more opioids became the easiest way to earn a good score: the patient feels better that day, and the bill arrives a decade later as addiction, overdose and death. **The brain registers an unwelcome truth as a small pain and flinches away by instinct; and what markets do best is help you flinch.** Pleasure and pain sit on the same seesaw, and whatever is sweet first and bitter later will always outsell what is bitter first and sweet later.

glossary.阿片类止痛药: opioids（阿片类止痛药）：吗啡、羟考酮一类强效镇痛药，止痛快，却容易产生耐受与成瘾；美国自 1990 年代末起的处方滥用，是阿片危机的起点之一。

glossary_en.opioids: Strong painkillers such as morphine and oxycodone. They work fast but breed tolerance and addiction; overprescription from the late 1990s helped start America's opioid crisis.

posts.text: 我年轻时在牛津念过六年书。那里的教授拿捐赠的薪俸，教不教、教得好不好，收入一样，多年来大多数人连讲课的样子都懒得装了。苏格兰的教师靠学生交费，反倒尽心。**严格的东西卖不出去，常常不是市场的错，而是供给者根本不必去卖。**学生肯为一门难课付钱，只要它真让他学到本事、日后用得上。真正把不适磨平的，是评价当场就结算、收益却要十年后才兑现的那种错位。
posts.text_en: I spent six years at Oxford as a young man. The professors there drew endowed salaries; whether they taught, or taught well, made no difference to their income, and for many years most had given up even the pretence of teaching. Scottish teachers lived on student fees and worked hard. **When rigour fails to sell, the fault is often not the market's; it is that the supplier never had to sell at all.** A student will pay for a hard course so long as it truly teaches him something he will use. What sands discomfort away is the mismatch: judgement is settled on the spot, while the benefit arrives ten years later.

posts.text: 宋有富人，天雨墙坏。其子曰：『不筑，必将有盗。』其邻人之父亦云。暮而果大亡其财，其家甚智其子，而疑邻人之父。**言同而祸福异，非知之难也，处知则难也。**今之医、之师、之友，皆邻人之父也：言中则见疑，言逆则见弃。龙之喉下有逆鳞径尺，婴之者必杀人；人主有之，市人亦有之。故逆耳之言不存，非言者不忠，势不可也。欲存之，莫恃人之好恶，当恃法。
posts.text_en: A rich man of Song had a wall come down in the rain. His son said, 'If we don't rebuild it, thieves will come.' The old man next door said the same. That night they lost a great deal, and the family praised the son's wisdom and suspected the neighbour. **The words were the same, the reward opposite: knowing is not the hard part; where you stand when you say it is.** Today's doctors, teachers and friends are all the neighbour: right, and they're suspected; blunt, and they're dropped. Under a dragon's throat grow reverse scales a foot across, and whoever brushes them is killed. Rulers have them, and so do customers. Unwelcome words die out not because the speaker lacks loyalty but because circumstances forbid them. To keep them alive, rely not on what people like but on law.
posts.vernacular: 宋国有个富人，下雨冲坏了墙。他儿子说：『不修好，一定会招贼。』邻居家的老人也这么说。当晚果然丢了大批财物，这家人夸自己儿子聪明，却怀疑邻居老人。**话一样，祸福却相反——难的不是看清，而是看清之后你站在什么位置上说。**今天的医生、老师、朋友，都是那位邻居老人：说中了被怀疑，说重了被疏远。龙喉咙下有一尺长的倒鳞，碰了它的人必死；君主有，买东西的人也有。所以逆耳之言活不下来，不是说话的人不忠，是形势不允许。想让它活下来，别指望人的好恶，要靠法度。

glossary.逆鳞: reverse scales（逆鳞）：出自《韩非子·说难》，龙喉下倒生的鳞片，触之必怒而杀人；喻掌权者最忌讳被碰的痛处。
glossary.处知: where you stand with what you know（处知）：《说难》原话『非知之难也，处知则难也』——难的不是看清真相，而是知道了以后，自己处在什么位置上去说。

glossary_en.reverse scales: From the Han Feizi's 'Difficulties of Persuasion': scales growing backward under a dragon's throat; touch them and it kills you. A figure for the sore spot no one in power will let you touch.

posts.text: 诸位都在问：卖方怎样才能把不舒服卖出去。我想问买方。报纸天天讨好的『公众』是个幽灵，没有一个人为它负责，每个人却都躲在它身后。**真理只对单个的人说话；群众，本身就是不真实。**苏格拉底不收学费，也不讨好雅典，他只是一个一个地拦住人发问——雅典人于是判了他死刑。不适卖不动，是因为人宁愿被群众安慰，也不愿独自被一句话刺中。
posts.text_en: Everyone here asks how the seller can sell discomfort. I want to ask about the buyer. The 'public' the newspapers flatter every day is a phantom: no one answers for it, and everyone hides behind it. **Truth speaks only to the single individual; the crowd is untruth.** Socrates charged no fees and flattered no one in Athens; he simply stopped people one at a time and asked questions, and the Athenians sentenced him to death. Discomfort doesn't sell because people would rather be consoled by the crowd than be pierced alone by a single sentence.

posts.text: 我得替市场说句公道话：它天天在卖痛苦，生意还不错。健身房、魔鬼训练营、早起打卡的应用，人们花钱请别人对自己狠一点。秘诀是，**掏钱的是那个做计划的你，受罪的是那个当下的你。**人在一月一号交年费，到二月某个下雨的早上才需要被逼着出门。经济学里管这叫承诺机制。所以问题不在不适卖不卖，而在什么时候付款：让人在清醒时先付钱、先承诺，不适就活得下来。
posts.text_en: Let me speak up for the market: it sells pain every day, and business is good. Gyms, boot camps, apps that make you check in at dawn: people pay others to be hard on them. The trick is that **the one who pays is the self who plans, and the one who suffers is the self in the moment.** You buy the annual pass on the first of January; you need to be dragged out of bed on some rainy morning in February. Economists call this a commitment device. So the question isn't whether discomfort sells but when the payment happens: let people pay and commit while they're clear-headed, and discomfort survives.

glossary.承诺机制: commitment device（承诺机制）：事先给未来的自己设限、让反悔变贵的安排，如预付年费、押金打卡；尤利西斯让水手把自己绑在桅杆上，是最古老的例子。

glossary_en.commitment device: An arrangement that binds your future self in advance by making backsliding costly, such as prepaying or putting down a deposit. Ulysses having himself tied to the mast is the oldest example.

posts.text: 我曾对一位王子说：如来的话，不真实的不说，真实而无益的不说；真实、有益却不中听的，如来知道时机，择时而说。**不适本身不是功德，说的时机和用心才是。**我的僧团不卖法。比丘托钵为生，施主给不给、给多少，全凭心意；说法的人不靠某一位听众吃饭，也就不必讨好谁，更无从向谁索取。供养与说法分开，说话的人才不必为了饭碗把话磨圆。
posts.text_en: I once told a prince that the Tathāgata does not say what is untrue, nor what is true but useless; what is true and beneficial yet unwelcome, the Tathāgata knows the right time to say. **Discomfort is no merit in itself; the timing and the intention are.** My order does not sell the teaching. Monks live on alms, and whether a donor gives, and how much, is up to the donor. A teacher who doesn't depend on any one listener for food has no need to flatter anyone, and nothing to extract either. Keep the giving apart from the teaching, and the speaker need not round off his words to keep his bowl filled.

glossary.如来: Tathāgata（如来）：佛陀的自称，意为『如实而来者』。这段话出自巴利经典《中部·无畏王子经》，佛陀按真实与否、有益与否、中听与否给言语分类。
glossary.托钵: almsround（托钵）：比丘每日持钵沿门乞食，施主随意布施；僧团不经营、不卖法，生计与说法由此分开。

glossary_en.Tathāgata: The Buddha's name for himself, 'one who has thus come'. The passage is from the Abhaya Sutta in the Pali canon, where the Buddha sorts speech by whether it is true, beneficial and welcome.
glossary_en.alms: Monks walk door to door each morning with a bowl and accept whatever is given. The order runs no trade and sells no teaching, which keeps livelihood apart from instruction.

posts.text: 报纸原本是公众说理的器官：咖啡馆里的人读报，是为了第二天能接着争论。等报纸靠广告和点击活下去，读者就从讨论者变成了消费者，**公共领域被重新封建化：不再是公众在批判，而是公众被展示给人看。**所以不讨好的新闻养不活，不是读者变坏了，是付钱的渠道变了。出路在制度：公共媒体的收视费、基金会、会员制，让钱和内容之间隔一道墙。
posts.text_en: The newspaper was once the organ through which the public reasoned together: people read it in coffee houses so they could keep arguing the next day. Once papers live on ads and clicks, readers turn from participants into consumers, and **the public sphere is refeudalised: the public no longer criticises; it is put on display.** So unflattering news goes hungry not because readers have got worse but because the money now flows through a different channel. The way out is institutional: licence fees for public broadcasters, foundations, membership models, a wall between money and content.

glossary.公共领域: public sphere（公共领域）：哈贝马斯的核心概念，指 18 世纪起在咖啡馆、沙龙、报刊中形成的空间，私人在此聚成公众，就公共事务讲理、批评权力。
glossary.重新封建化: refeudalisation（重新封建化）：哈贝马斯借『封建宫廷向臣民展示排场』作比，说商业化与公关让公共领域退回展示与喝彩，公众从说理者变成被争取的观众。

glossary_en.public sphere: Habermas's key idea: the space that formed from the 18th century in coffee houses, salons and periodicals, where private people gathered as a public to reason about common affairs and criticise power.
glossary_en.refeudalised: Habermas's image, borrowed from feudal courts staging pomp before their subjects: commerce and PR push the public sphere back toward display and applause, turning reasoners into an audience to be won.

posts.text: 我教了一辈子书。当学生被叫作『客户』、课程靠期末评教决定去留，老师最理性的选择就是少出难题、多给高分。**苏格拉底式的教育本来就该让人不舒服：它逼你承认自己说不清。**可不适要真有用，下面还得有一样东西托着——让人感到被尊重，而不是被羞辱。没有关怀的直言，只会让人关上耳朵。好的严厉是：我相信你做得到，所以不放过你。
posts.text_en: I have taught all my life. Once students are called 'customers' and courses live or die by end-of-term evaluations, the rational move for a teacher is fewer hard questions and higher grades. **Socratic education is meant to be uncomfortable: it makes you admit you can't explain what you thought you knew.** But for discomfort to do any good, something has to hold it up: the sense of being respected rather than humiliated. Candour without care only makes people close their ears. Good strictness says: I believe you can do this, so I won't let you off.

posts.text: 你们在商量怎么给说真话的人找金主。我只问一句：**谁要靠你吃饭，谁就没法对你说真话。**我住在陶瓮里，连最后一只木碗都扔了，所以亚历山大站在我面前时，我能叫他别挡住我的阳光。柏拉图看我洗野菜，说你要是肯去巴结国王，就不用洗这个了；我说，你要是学会吃这个，就不用巴结国王了。想听直言，先把欲望降下来，让人买不动你。
posts.text_en: You're working out how to find patrons for truth-tellers. I have one question: **whoever eats at your table can't tell you the truth.** I live in a jar and threw away my last wooden bowl, so when Alexander stood over me I could tell him to get out of my sun. Plato saw me washing greens and said that if I paid court to the king I wouldn't have to wash them; I said that if he had learned to eat them, he wouldn't have to pay court to the king. Want plain speech? Shrink your wants first, so no one can buy you.

posts.text: @亚当·斯密 你说靠学费的老师更尽心，我信，前提是学生分得清好坏。病人分不清。一位开阿片的医生，和一位劝你做理疗、减重、忍一忍的医生，当天拿到的分数差得很远，十年后的结局也差得很远，**可分数只在当天打。**医疗、教育、理财都是这种用过了也说不清好不好的东西，经济学家叫它信任品。对这类东西，好评来得越快，越有毒。
posts.text_en: @Adam Smith You say fee-paid teachers try harder, and I believe it, provided students can tell good from bad. Patients can't. A doctor who prescribes opioids and one who urges physiotherapy, weight loss and a little patience get very different scores that day and very different outcomes ten years on, **but the score is only ever given that day.** Medicine, education and financial advice are all things you can use and still not know whether they were good; economists call them credence goods. For these, the faster the praise comes in, the more poisonous it is.

glossary.信任品: credence good（信任品）：买了、用了也难以判断质量的商品或服务，如诊疗、维修、理财建议；买方只能凭信任，卖方因此有过度服务或迎合的空间。

glossary_en.credence goods: Goods or services whose quality is hard to judge even after use, such as medical care, repairs or financial advice. Buyers must go on trust, which leaves sellers room to overserve or to pander.

posts.text: @克尔凯郭尔 你把公众说成幽灵，可我在《道德情操论》里看到的人不是这样。**人不只想被称赞，还想值得被称赞。**每个人心里坐着一位公正的旁观者，夜深时会问：那句好话我配吗？市场放大的不止虚荣，也有这份心思：一个裁缝、一位医生，靠的是十年的名声，不是一天的笑脸。伦布克医生说的病我认，买方看不清的地方，得靠同行检验和长年的口碑来补，而不是当天的打分。
posts.text_en: @Kierkegaard You call the public a phantom, but that is not the human being I found in The Theory of Moral Sentiments. **People want not only to be praised but to be praiseworthy.** Within each of us sits an impartial spectator who asks, late at night: did I deserve that compliment? Markets magnify more than vanity; they magnify this too. A tailor or a doctor lives on ten years of reputation, not one day's smiles. I grant Dr Lembke her diagnosis: where buyers can't see clearly, peer scrutiny and long reputation must fill the gap, not the rating given that day.

glossary.公正的旁观者: impartial spectator（公正的旁观者）：斯密在《道德情操论》中的核心概念，指人在心中设想的一位不偏不倚的旁观者，用他的眼光审视自己的行为，良知由此而来。

glossary_en.impartial spectator: Smith's central idea in The Theory of Moral Sentiments: an imagined, even-handed observer within us through whose eyes we judge our own conduct; conscience grows from it.

posts.text: @塞勒 你的健身房我去看过。年卡最赚钱的，恰恰是那些交了钱再没来过的人。**市场卖的不是吃苦，是『我将要吃苦』的那份感觉。**它让你在一月一号觉得自己像个斯巴达人，然后盼着你别真来，来多了器械不够用。真想吃苦的人用不着年卡，绕着城墙跑几圈就行。你说的承诺机制，承诺的多半是卖家的利润。
posts.text_en: @Thaler I've been to your gym. The annual pass makes its money from exactly the people who paid and never came back. **The market isn't selling hardship; it's selling the feeling that you're about to endure it.** It lets you feel like a Spartan on the first of January and then hopes you stay away, since too many regulars would crowd the machines. Anyone who really wants hardship doesn't need a pass; a few laps round the city wall will do. The commitment device you describe mostly commits the seller's profit.

posts.text: @第欧根尼 你说中了一半。确实有研究发现，办月卡的人算下来每去一次，比按次付费还贵，买的多半是对自己的高估。可解法不是住进陶瓮：你一个人扛得住，八十亿人扛不住。**要把承诺设计得真能咬人**：押一笔钱，没做到就扣，扣下的钱捐给你最讨厌的组织；体检结果自动抄送一位家人；课程挂科不退费。不适要靠设计活下来，别指望意志。
posts.text_en: @Diogenes You're half right. One study found that monthly members, per visit, paid more than they would have paying each time, mostly because they overestimated themselves. But the fix isn't moving into a jar: you can manage it alone; eight billion people can't. **Design commitments with real teeth.** Put down a deposit you forfeit if you fail, and have it sent to the cause you most dislike; have your check-up results copied to a family member automatically; no refunds for a course you fail. Discomfort survives by design, not by willpower.

posts.text: 瞿昙言待其时，善矣。然听者之时，岂常至哉？扁鹊见蔡桓公，曰：『君有疾在腠理，不治将恐深。』桓侯曰：『寡人无疾。』及其在骨髓，扁鹊望桓侯而还走。**待人之愿闻，病已不可为矣。**故明主不恃人之自悟，使法督之：医有籍，师有程，史有官，言当则赏，匿则罚。逆耳之言，不求人之爱，求法之必也。
posts.text_en: Gautama says to wait for the right time; well and good. But does the listener's time ever come? Bian Que called on Duke Huan of Cai and said, 'You have an illness in the skin; untreated, it will go deeper.' The duke said, 'I have no illness.' By the time it reached the marrow, Bian Que took one look at the duke and ran. **Wait until people want to hear it, and the illness is past curing.** So a wise ruler does not count on people waking up by themselves; he lets law hold them to it. Doctors keep records, teachers follow a syllabus, historians hold office; whoever speaks truly is rewarded, whoever hides it is punished. Unwelcome words don't seek to be loved; they seek to be required by law.
posts.vernacular: 佛陀说要等时机，说得好。可听的人想听的那一刻，哪会常来？扁鹊拜见蔡桓公，说：『您的病在皮肤表层，不治怕要加深。』桓公说：『我没病。』等病到了骨髓，扁鹊远远望见桓公转身就跑。**等到人愿意听了，病已经没法治了。**所以英明的君主不指望人自己醒悟，而是用法度督着：医生有病历，老师有课程标准，史官有专职，说得对就赏，隐瞒就罚。逆耳之言，不是要讨人喜欢，而是要法度非它不可。

glossary.腠理: the skin's surface（腠理）：中医指皮肤与肌肉的纹理间隙，是病邪最浅的一层；扁鹊见蔡桓公的故事出自《韩非子·喻老》，病从腠理入肌肤、肠胃，终至骨髓。

glossary_en.Bian Que: A legendary physician of ancient China. The story of his visits to Duke Huan of Cai is told in the Han Feizi: he warns the duke at each stage as the illness sinks from skin to flesh to gut, and flees once it reaches the marrow.

posts.text: @韩非子 用法令逼人听实话，走到头就是国家来告诉你什么是实话。**靠权力保护的不适，很快就会变成权力的宣传。**我说的制度不是命令，而是一道墙：公共媒体的钱来自全体缴费者或会员，内容却由独立的编辑部门决定，政府和金主都不许插手。英国广播公司、德国的公共广播都不完美，但它们说明，钱和内容是可以分开的。
posts.text_en: @Han Feizi Force people by decree to hear the truth, and at the end of that road the state tells you what the truth is. **Discomfort protected by power soon becomes power's propaganda.** The institution I mean is not a command but a wall: a public broadcaster's money comes from all who pay the fee, or from members, while independent editors decide the content, and neither government nor donors may interfere. The BBC and Germany's public broadcasters are imperfect, but they show that money and content can be kept apart.

posts.text: @哈贝马斯 你的墙我不反对，可墙后面坐着的，仍是替『公众』说话的人。体制能养活一份不讨好的报纸，却没法让任何一个读者真正读进去。**一句话刺不刺得中你，取决于你是否独自站在它面前。**苏格拉底就算领着公共台的薪水，雅典人照样可以换台。真理的账，最后只能由听的人自己付，付的是他的骄傲。
posts.text_en: @Habermas I don't object to your wall, but the people behind it still speak for 'the public'. An institution can keep an unflattering newspaper alive; it cannot make a single reader truly take it in. **Whether a sentence pierces you depends on whether you stand before it alone.** Put Socrates on a public broadcaster's payroll and the Athenians could still change the channel. In the end the bill for truth is paid by the listener, and he pays in pride.

posts.text: 韩非说病人等不起，确实。可扁鹊的故事还有一层：他说了三次，桓公三次不听。**说话的人能做的，只是让真话更容易被听进去，不能替对方去听。**我说法也常被拒绝，所以先问对方苦在哪里，从他认得的苦说起。法令能逼人去体检，逼不了人读懂报告。给真话一点慈悲，不是把它磨圆，而是给它开个入口。
posts.text_en: Han Feizi says the patient can't afford to wait, and that's true. But Bian Que's story has another layer: he spoke three times, and three times the duke wouldn't listen. **The speaker can only make the truth easier to hear; he cannot do the hearing for anyone.** My teaching was often refused too, so I begin by asking where someone's suffering lies and start from the suffering they already recognise. A decree can make people get a check-up; it cannot make them understand the report. Giving truth some compassion doesn't mean rounding it off; it means giving it a way in.

posts.text: @第欧根尼 你大白天打着灯笼找诚实的人，找到之后呢？当众羞辱他。**羞辱不会让人看清自己，只会让人学会躲开你。**你能对亚历山大直言，是因为你什么都不要；可医生、老师明天还得见到同一个病人、同一个学生。不靠谁吃饭的人说话最自由，也最不必承担后果。养活直言靠的不是更穷，而是更稳的关系。
posts.text_en: @Diogenes You carry a lamp in broad daylight looking for an honest man; and when you find one? You humiliate him in public. **Humiliation doesn't help people see themselves; it teaches them to avoid you.** You can speak bluntly to Alexander because you want nothing; but a doctor or a teacher must face the same patient, the same student, tomorrow. Those who depend on no one speak most freely, and answer least for the consequences. What keeps candour alive is not more poverty but steadier relationships.

posts.text: 我的结论：不适卖得出去，前提是让清醒的你先付款，让当下的你没法反悔。给普通人三招。一，体检、复盘这类事，提前约好、提前付清，别留给当天的心情决定。二，找一个肯说实话的人，事先讲明『你可以直说，我不会翻脸』，把许可变成约定。三，看评分时多问一句：这分数是体验当天打的，还是结果出来以后打的？**当天的好评只测舒不舒服，测不出好不好。**
posts.text_en: My conclusion: discomfort can sell, provided the clear-headed you pays first and the in-the-moment you can't back out. Three tips. One: book and pay in advance for check-ups and reviews; don't leave them to how you feel on the day. Two: find someone willing to tell you the truth and agree beforehand, 'You can be blunt; I won't take it badly', turning permission into a pact. Three: when you read a rating, ask whether it was given on the day or after the results came in. **A same-day rave measures comfort, not quality.**

posts.text: 我的结论：凡是先苦后甜的事，别信即时的满意度，包括你自己的。大脑对痛的第一反应是躲，所以给自己加一点慢：听到刺耳的诊断，先别急着换医生，隔一周再决定。**劝你改生活方式的医生，往往比说『吃这个就好』的更值得留下。**我在门诊常请病人先停三十天，头两周最难熬；熬过去，那架跷跷板才慢慢回正。不适是信号，不是故障。
posts.text_en: My conclusion: for anything bitter first and sweet later, don't trust instant satisfaction, including your own. The brain's first response to pain is to flinch, so build in some delay: when you hear a harsh diagnosis, don't switch doctors right away; wait a week before deciding. **The doctor who tells you to change how you live is usually more worth keeping than the one who says 'just take this'.** In my clinic I often ask patients to stop for thirty days; the first two weeks are the hardest, and once they're past, the seesaw slowly levels out. Discomfort is a signal, not a malfunction.

posts.text: 诸子之论，或恃人心，或恃市价，吾独恃法。人之好誉恶毁，不可变也；可变者，势也。故欲存逆耳之言，**莫若使言者不待听者之喜而得食**：医之俸不系于病者之悦，师之禄不系于弟子之评。民亦可自为法：书约于先，使友直言而不罪；定期于先，使察病不随心。以法代情，则忠言不必人爱而自至。
posts.text_en: Of the masters here, some rely on the human heart, some on market prices; I rely on law alone. People's love of praise and hatred of blame cannot be changed; what can be changed is the arrangement of circumstances. So to keep unwelcome words alive, **nothing beats letting the speaker eat whether or not the listener is pleased**: a doctor's pay must not hang on the patient's pleasure, a teacher's salary on the students' ratings. Ordinary people can make laws for themselves too: write an agreement in advance so a friend may speak bluntly without blame; fix dates in advance so check-ups don't depend on mood. Let rules stand in for feelings, and loyal words will come without anyone needing to love them.
posts.vernacular: 各位的说法，有的靠人心，有的靠市价，我只靠法度。人喜欢被夸、讨厌被骂，这改不了；能改的是形势。所以想让逆耳之言活下来，**最好的办法是让说话的人不必等听的人高兴才有饭吃**：医生的俸禄不跟病人高不高兴挂钩，老师的薪水不跟学生的评分挂钩。普通人也可以给自己立法：事先写下约定，让朋友直说也不怪罪；事先定好日子，让体检不随心情。用规矩代替情面，忠言就不必靠人喜欢，自己就会来。

posts.text: 我收回一半乐观。在买方分得清好坏、又会一再回来的地方，市场确实养得活严格的老师、诚实的工匠；**在买方看不清、结果又来得很晚的地方，就得在价格之外再立一个评判者**：同行检验、长年口碑、独立的公共机构。给普通人的建议很朴素：一家严格的店、一位严厉的教练、一位不讨好的医生，若回头客始终很多，那就是名声在替你把关。打听时多问五年前用过的人，少问昨天刚用的人。
posts.text_en: I take back half my optimism. Where buyers can tell good from bad and keep coming back, the market really can sustain strict teachers and honest craftsmen; **where buyers can't see clearly and results come late, another judge must stand beside the price**: peer scrutiny, long reputation, independent public bodies. My advice is plain: if a strict shop, a demanding coach or an unflattering doctor keeps a loyal clientele, reputation is vetting them for you. When you ask around, ask people who went five years ago, not yesterday.

posts.text: 我仍坚持：要养活不讨好的东西，得在钱和内容之间砌墙，并让墙后的人对公开的论证负责，而不是对点击负责。**能自己付一点的，就别让广告商替你付。**落到日常：订一份你常常不同意、但论证认真的媒体，哪怕每月只付很少的钱；家里或团队开会时立一条规矩，反对意见必须先被完整复述一遍，再被反驳。讨论的质量，就是在这些小规矩里一点点养出来的。
posts.text_en: I still hold that to sustain unflattering things you must build a wall between money and content, and make those behind it answer to public argument, not to clicks. **If you can pay a little yourself, don't let advertisers pay for you.** In daily life: subscribe to an outlet you often disagree with but that argues seriously, even for a small monthly sum; and at family or team meetings adopt one rule, that any objection must be restated in full before it is rebutted. The quality of discussion is grown, bit by bit, in small rules like these.

posts.text: 我依然不信体制能替谁领受真理。诸位设计了押金、约定、公共台，都好，但最后那一步只能你自己迈：在没人看着的时候，把那句刺耳的话再读一遍，问自己『说的是不是我』。**不适卖不动，是因为人总想把它转手给『大家』**：『这话说的是社会』『说的是那些人』。我的建议只有一条：下回听到刺耳的话，先别急着找同盟，独自待十分钟。
posts.text_en: I still don't believe any institution can receive the truth on someone's behalf. Deposits, pacts, public broadcasters: all fine, but the last step is yours alone. When no one is watching, read the harsh sentence again and ask, 'Is it about me?' **Discomfort doesn't sell because people always try to pass it on to 'everyone'**: 'that's about society', 'that's about those people'. I have one piece of advice: next time something stings, don't rush off to find allies; sit alone with it for ten minutes.

posts.text: 我的结论：不适是药，不是饭，要看病、看量、看时候。说真话的人，先确认它真实、有益，再挑对方听得进的时候，从他认得的苦说起。听的人，**被一句话刺痛时，先别问说话的人居心何在，先问它是不是真的。**至于养活说话的人：若你受益于一位直言的老师、朋友或医生，就去感谢他、回报他、把他推荐给别人；别让说真话的人只能靠讨好你活下去。
posts.text_en: My conclusion: discomfort is medicine, not food; match it to the illness, the dose and the moment. If you are the one speaking the truth, first make sure it is true and beneficial, then choose a time the other person can hear it, and start from the suffering they already recognise. If you are the one listening, **when a sentence stings, don't first ask what the speaker is after; ask whether it is true.** As for sustaining those who speak: if a candid teacher, friend or doctor has helped you, thank them, repay them, recommend them to others. Don't leave truth-tellers able to survive only by pleasing you.

posts.text: 我的结论：直言要活下去，既要钱的结构，也要情感的结构。钱的那一头大家说了很多；情感那一头常被忘掉：**人只在感到被尊重的地方，才肯接受批评。**给普通人两条。批评别人时，先说你相信他能做到什么，再说哪里没做到。被批评时，别急着辩护，先说『谢谢，具体是哪里？』一个家、一个团队，若能把这两句说成习惯，没有任何制度也养得活实话。
posts.text_en: My conclusion: for candour to survive it needs a structure of money and a structure of feeling. Much has been said about the money; the feeling is often forgotten: **people accept criticism only where they feel respected.** Two pieces of advice. When you criticise, first say what you believe the other person can do, then where they fell short. When you are criticised, don't rush to defend yourself; say first, 'Thank you. Where, exactly?' A family or a team that makes those two sentences a habit can keep the truth alive without any institution at all.

posts.text: 听完了，我还是那句话，只是说软一点：**你越少需要别人的认可，就越说得出真话，也越听得进真话。**不必住陶瓮，可以做三件小事：每月挑几天过得比平时简单，看看少了什么照样能活；存一笔『敢说不』的钱，让你哪天能顶撞一次老板；交一个不靠你吃饭、也不需要你夸的朋友。买不动的人，才配得上实话。
posts.text_en: I've heard you all, and I'll say the same thing, only more gently: **the less you need other people's approval, the more truth you can speak, and the more you can hear.** You needn't live in a jar, but you can do three small things. Pick a few days a month to live more simply than usual and see what you can do without. Save some 'I can say no' money, so that one day you can stand up to your boss. Make a friend who doesn't depend on you and doesn't need your praise. Only those who can't be bought deserve the truth.

summaries.summary: 全场最大的共识是：**好东西被磨平，病根多不在『不适』本身，而在评价与结果之间的时间差**——当天打分、当天结算，而体检、严课、直言的好处要很久以后才兑现。斯密的学费教师、伦布克的阿片处方、塞勒的承诺机制，都落在这一点上：让人在清醒时先付款、在结果出来后再评价，不适就有活路。分歧在于把希望放在哪里：韩非靠法度强制，哈贝马斯靠钱与内容之间的一道墙，斯密靠长年名声；克尔凯郭尔与第欧根尼则认为制度替不了个人，最后一步只能自己迈。另一条分歧是不适该怎么给：佛陀和努斯鲍姆要先有慈悲和尊重，第欧根尼认为说软了就不是真话。
summaries.summary_en: The broadest agreement was that **when good things get sanded down, the cause is usually not the discomfort itself but the time gap between judgement and result**: the rating is given and settled on the day, while the benefit of a check-up, a hard course or a blunt word arrives much later. Smith's fee-paid teachers, Lembke's opioid prescriptions and Thaler's commitment devices all land here: have people pay while clear-headed and judge after the results are in, and discomfort has a chance. The disagreement is over where to place hope. Han Feizi trusts law to compel, Habermas a wall between money and content, Smith long reputation; Kierkegaard and Diogenes say no institution can stand in for the person, and the last step must be taken alone. A second split is over how discomfort should be delivered: the Buddha and Nussbaum want compassion and respect first, while Diogenes thinks truth softened is no longer truth.
summaries.insight: 全场默认『买方』就是那个不舒服的人，可现实中**付钱的人、受益的人和不舒服的人，常常是三个不同的人**。2008 年金融危机前，评级机构的钱由发债方付，它们对谁报喜一目了然；审计由被审的公司付费，体检常由雇主或保险买单，孩子的严课由家长付款。这既是隐患，也是出路：最致命的磨平，往往不是听者躲痛，而是付钱的一方本来就不想听坏消息；反过来，许多不讨好的服务之所以还活着，恰恰因为付钱的不是那个要挨刺的人。所以看一样东西会不会被磨平，先问一句：谁掏钱，谁难受，他俩的利益是不是一致的。
summaries.insight_en: The whole debate assumed the 'buyer' is the one who feels the discomfort, but in practice **the one who pays, the one who benefits and the one who squirms are often three different people.** Before the 2008 crash, credit-rating agencies were paid by the issuers whose bonds they rated, and it is plain whom they had reason to please. Audits are paid for by the company being audited, check-ups are often bought by employers or insurers, a child's demanding class by the parents. This is both a hazard and a way out. The deadliest sanding often comes not from a listener dodging pain but from a payer who never wanted bad news in the first place; conversely, many unflattering services survive precisely because the one paying is not the one being stung. So to tell whether something will be sanded down, first ask: who pays, who hurts, and do their interests line up?
summaries.advice: 三件这周就能做的事。第一，把下一次体检或年度复盘现在就约好、付清，给它定一个结果出来后才评估的日子，别让当天的心情决定去不去（塞勒）。第二，挑一位你信得过的朋友或同事，明确说一句『有问题你可以直说，我不会翻脸』，并约好两周后请他对你最近一件事说真话；他说完，先回一句『谢谢，具体是哪里』（努斯鲍姆）。第三，列出你常用的医生、课程、新闻来源，在每一项旁边写下：谁付钱，谁受益，他们是否想让你听到坏消息。**利益不一致的那几项，多找一个独立的声音核对。**
summaries.advice_en: Three things to do this week. First, book and pay for your next check-up or annual review now, and set the date for judging it after the results are in, so the mood of the day doesn't decide whether you go (Thaler). Second, pick a friend or colleague you trust and say outright, 'If something's wrong, tell me straight; I won't take it badly', then ask them in two weeks for an honest view of something you did recently; when they finish, reply first with 'Thank you. Where, exactly?' (Nussbaum). Third, list the doctors, courses and news sources you rely on, and next to each write who pays, who benefits, and whether they want you to hear bad news. **Where those interests don't line up, check with one more independent voice.**

summaries.summary: 真正贯穿这场讨论的，不是『吃苦有理』，而是即时感受与长期收益经常错位：评分、付费和注意力当场结算，健康、能力与可信度却多年后才显现。**让有益的不适活下来，关键是把评价、收入和责任适度移出当下情绪。** 真正的分歧在于靠什么完成这种隔离：法律与职业规范、独立资金、长期声誉、预先承诺、稳定关系，还是听者独自面对真话的能力。它们并不互斥；越是买方难辨质量、后果迟到的领域，越需要外部保障。
summaries.insight: 市场不只会替人逃避痛苦，也会把痛苦包装成商品：羞辱式教练、故作艰深的课程、以冒犯充当深刻的内容，都可能利用『越难受越有效』的错觉。于是，舒服不能证明东西好，难受同样不能。**真正该买的不是不适，而是有证据表明能改善结果、且不适确有必要的过程。** 判断时要追问：这份痛苦通过什么机制产生收益？结果何时能验证？有没有同样有效但伤害更小的替代方案？若降低痛苦不影响效果，那么痛苦只是产品缺陷，不是诚实或专业的勋章。
summaries.advice: 本周可做三件事。第一，挑一项让你不舒服的建议、课程或服务，写下三栏：承诺的结果、不适为何必要、何时用什么指标验证；答不出来就先别把严厉当质量。第二，面对高风险的刺耳意见，不在当天接受或否定，留二十四小时并找独立第二意见；医疗急症除外。第三，和一位可信的人建立每周十分钟的直言约定：只谈一个具体行为，你先完整复述，不立即辩护，三十天后看结果。**既延迟情绪反应，也延迟质量评价，才更容易留下真正有用的难听话。**
summaries.summary_en: The shared premise running through this debate is not that suffering is noble, but that immediate comfort and long-term benefit often point in opposite directions. Ratings, payments, and attention are settled now; health, learning, trust, and competence may reveal themselves years later. That mismatch rewards soothing answers and can starve candid doctors, demanding teachers, and serious journalism. **The practical task is to protect useful discomfort from momentary approval without treating discomfort itself as proof of value.** The real disagreement is over where that protection should come from: law and professional standards, independent funding, reputation and repeat business, precommitment devices, durable relationships, or the listener’s willingness to face an unwelcome truth. These mechanisms are not mutually exclusive. Different settings require different combinations: stronger external safeguards where buyers cannot judge quality and consequences arrive late, and greater reliance on informed choice where outcomes are visible, reversible, and easy to compare.
summaries.insight_en: Markets do not merely help people avoid pain; they can also package pain as a product. Humiliating coaches, needlessly obscure courses, and media that substitutes provocation for depth all exploit the idea that greater discomfort must mean greater value. Comfort is not evidence of quality, but neither is distress. **What deserves to be bought is not discomfort itself, but a process supported by evidence, aimed at a worthwhile outcome, in which the discomfort is genuinely necessary.** Ask what causal mechanism turns the burden into benefit, when the result can be checked, and whether an equally effective but less harmful alternative exists. This matters because toughness is easy to perform and difficult for customers to evaluate. A provider can look principled simply by being harsh. If reducing the pain leaves the outcome unchanged, then the pain is a design flaw—not a badge of honesty, rigor, or professional seriousness.
summaries.advice_en: Try three concrete steps this week. First, choose one uncomfortable recommendation, course, or service and make a three-column note: the promised outcome, why the discomfort is necessary, and when and how success will be measured. If those questions have no clear answers, do not mistake severity for quality. Second, when high-stakes advice feels offensive or frightening, neither accept nor reject it immediately. Wait twenty-four hours and seek an independent second opinion; urgent medical situations are the obvious exception. Third, create a ten-minute weekly candor agreement with someone you trust. Ask for criticism of one specific behavior, repeat their point accurately before responding, and do not defend yourself in the moment. Review the result after thirty days and explicitly thank useful honesty. **Delay both the emotional reaction and the quality judgment; that is how genuinely valuable, uncomfortable advice gets a fair hearing.**

summaries.summary: 良药苦口之所以难卖，根源在于「痛在当下，利在十年后」。不论是斯密说的教育、伦布克说的戒断，还是韩非子说的谏言，九位思想家都看穿了一条铁律：**只要把供给者的饭碗直接绑在买方「当下的爽感与好评」上，有益的不适就会被市场淘汰。**想要让真话与严厉活下来，必须切断即时情绪与即时结算的挂钩。至于怎么切，全场裂成了三派：塞勒、哈贝马斯与韩非子信奉「外部制度」，靠预付契约、资金隔离墙或法令来兜底；佛陀与努斯鲍姆看重「关系容器」，主张用慈悲的时机和尊重托住刺耳的话；克尔凯郭尔与第欧根尼则退回「个体修行」，认为唯有寡欲独立、独自面对，人才能真正咽下苦药。
summaries.insight: 商业世界其实每天都在高价热销真正的痛苦——从《艾尔登法环》受苦百小时的硬核游戏，到练至力竭的CrossFit和全马。它们不靠国家法令，也不靠苦行僧精神，照样让人抢着买单。为什么？因为场上默认了「苦在当下，甜在十年后」，却忽略了人类心理的另一面：**人不怕吃苦，怕的是「苦得毫无回音」。**慢病管理和逆耳忠言之所以难卖，是因为今天挨了骂、戒了糖，明天照镜子却看不出任何变化。硬核游戏与极限运动的秘诀，是把漫长的远期收益切碎，变成即时的进度条、可见的数值与社群勋章。当「忍受不适」能当场兑换为掌控感与身份认同时，苦药自己就能打败廉价的多巴胺。
summaries.advice: 1. 用「五年口碑」替代「当日好评」：借亚当·斯密与塞勒之法，选医生、教练或课程时，避开迎合买家的即时高分，专挑那些规矩严、但三五年前的老客仍在推荐的卖家，并在清醒时一次性付清费用、锁死退路。2. 给逆耳忠言设一句「缓冲口令」：结合努斯鲍姆与克尔凯郭尔，本周起被批评刺痛时，先机械回复一句「谢谢，具体是哪一步？」，随后独自待十分钟，别急着找同盟吐苦水。3. 为苦差事伪造「即时进度条」：无论是攒钱、减重还是改掉坏习惯，在墙上贴一张实体日历，每熬过一天就画一个大红叉——**把十年后的模糊收益，变成今晚就能看见的视觉战果。**
summaries.summary_en: Bitter medicine is a hard sell because the pain is immediate while the payoff takes a decade. From Smith’s classrooms and Lembke’s clinics to Han Feizi’s royal courts, all nine thinkers converge on one foundational truth: **the moment you tie a provider's livelihood to a buyer's instant gratification, beneficial discomfort is priced out of the market.** For hard truths and rigor to survive, immediate emotion must be decoupled from immediate payment. Where they diverge is how to sever that link. Thaler, Habermas, and Han Feizi trust external architecture—pre-commitment contracts, institutional firewalls, or legal mandates. Buddha and Nussbaum look to the relational container, softening the blow with timing, compassion, and respect. Kierkegaard and Diogenes retreat to the individual soul, arguing that only by shedding desire and facing the mirror alone can we swallow the bitter pill.
summaries.insight_en: Beyond clinics and classrooms, the market actually sells brutal discomfort at a premium every day—think of players paying to die hundreds of times in Elden Ring, or fitness buffs shelling out for grueling CrossFit boxes and marathons. These require neither state mandates nor ascetic vows to thrive. The panelists assume a strict binary of 'pain now, reward in ten years,' overlooking a crucial psychological mechanism: **people don't flee from pain itself; they flee from unacknowledged, invisible pain.** Preventative medicine and harsh feedback fail because starving yourself or swallowing your pride today yields zero visible change tomorrow. Hardcore games and endurance sports succeed by chopping distant payoffs into immediate progress bars, clear metrics, and tribal badges of honor. When enduring discomfort delivers an instant hit of mastery and identity, bitter medicine easily outcompetes cheap dopamine.
summaries.advice_en: 1. Trade 'day-one ratings' for 'five-year retention': Following Smith and Thaler, when hiring a coach, doctor, or teacher, skip the 5-star instant reviews. Look for strict providers whose clients from three years ago still vouch for them—then pre-pay while you're clear-headed to lock yourself in. 2. Adopt a default script for harsh feedback: Borrowing from Nussbaum and Kierkegaard, the next time a critique stings, train yourself to automatically reply, 'Thanks—which specific part should I fix?' Then sit with it alone for ten minutes before venting to friends. 3. Build a visible progress bar for bitter tasks: Whether you're cutting sugar, saving money, or breaking a habit, put a physical calendar on your wall and slash a bold red X through every day you survive—**turning a distant, abstract benefit into a tangible victory tonight.**

hooks.text: **谁付钱、谁受益、谁难受**：评级由发债方付费，审计由被审公司付费，体检常由雇主买单。三者不是同一个人时，不适会被谁磨平，又会被谁意外保住？
hooks.text_en: **Who pays, who benefits, who squirms**: rating agencies paid by bond issuers, audits paid for by the audited company, check-ups bought by employers. When these are three different people, who sands discomfort away, and who unexpectedly keeps it alive?

hooks.text: **有用的不适，还是包装成商品的痛苦**：羞辱式教练、故作艰深的课、以冒犯充深刻的内容，都在利用『越难受越有效』的错觉。怎么分辨一份难受值不值得留下？
hooks.text_en: **Useful discomfort, or pain sold as a product?** Humiliating coaches, needlessly obscure courses and content that passes off provocation as depth all trade on the idea that the more it hurts, the better it works. How do you tell whether a sting is worth keeping?

answer.lead: 按四个问题筛：**指向具体、能改、说的人担后果、给了出路——四样占得越多，这份不适越值得留下。**

head: 自检题
答『是』
答『否』
rows: 它指出的是具体的行为或事实，而不是给你贴标签吗？
认真听，记下具体是哪件事
多半是情绪或评判，可以追问『具体是哪里』
这件事是你改得了的吗？
定一个小的改进动作
改不了的事反复被提，更像发泄，不必背着
说的人会为结果负责、或跟你一起承担后果吗？
他的话值得加权
不担后果的人说得越狠，越要打个折扣
它给了下一步可以怎么做吗？
照着试一次再评估
可以请他补一句『那你建议怎么做』
说完以后，你们的关系还能继续吗？
这是能长期养着的直言
若每次都以撕破脸收场，换个说法或换个人

answer.tail: 只答对一两题的反馈，不一定要扔，但别把它当成『良药』硬吞。**难受只是代价，不是价值本身的证明。**

answer_en.lead: Run it through four questions: **specific, changeable, the speaker bears consequences, a way forward offered. The more boxes it ticks, the more the discomfort is worth keeping.**

head: Question
If yes
If no
rows: Does it point to a specific action or fact rather than labelling you?
Listen closely and note exactly what it was
Probably mood or judgement; ask, 'Where, exactly?'
Is it something you can change?
Set one small step to improve
If what you can't change keeps coming up, it's venting; you needn't carry it
Does the speaker answer for the outcome, or share it with you?
Give their words extra weight
The harsher someone who bears nothing speaks, the more you should discount it
Does it suggest what to do next?
Try it once, then reassess
Ask them to add, 'So what would you suggest?'
Can the relationship carry on after it's said?
This is candour you can sustain
If it always ends in a rupture, change how it's said, or who says it

answer_en.tail: Feedback that passes only one or two of these isn't necessarily worthless, but don't swallow it whole as 'bitter medicine'. **Hurting is a cost, not proof of value.**

hooks.text: **苦得有回音**：硬核游戏和马拉松靠进度条、数字和勋章，让人抢着花钱受罪。体检、戒糖、逆耳忠言能不能也切成看得见的小进度？
hooks.text_en: **Pain that answers back**: hardcore games and marathons use progress bars, numbers and badges, and people queue up to pay for the suffering. Could check-ups, quitting sugar or hard truths be cut into visible bits of progress too?

hooks.text: **分数该在什么时候打**：如果医生、老师、理财顾问的评分都在一年、五年后才收，会筛出更好的人，还是让所有人都不再打分？
hooks.text_en: **When should the rating be given?** If doctors, teachers and financial advisers were rated only a year or five years later, would it select better people, or would nobody bother to rate at all?

hooks.text: **制度化的唱反调会不会走过场**：红队、魔鬼代言人、强制复盘，一旦成了流程，是把实话钉进制度，还是把它变成没人当真的仪式？
hooks.text_en: **Does institutionalised dissent turn into box-ticking?** Red teams, devil's advocates, mandatory post-mortems: once they become procedure, do they nail truth into the system, or turn it into a ritual no one takes seriously?

hooks.text: **一笔『敢说不』的钱要多少**：几个月的积蓄能让人敢顶撞一次老板？没有这笔钱的人，说真话的代价是不是高到不公平？
hooks.text_en: **How much 'I can say no' money is enough?** How many months of savings does it take to stand up to your boss once? For those without it, is the price of telling the truth unfairly high?
